title: 34. Capstone: Operate a Linux Service
content:
# 34. Capstone: Operate a Linux Service

This capstone combines the course into one realistic operational workflow. The goal is not to run every command you know. The goal is to reason clearly, change carefully, and verify with evidence.

## Scenario

You own a Linux host running an HTTP API behind a proxy. Users report intermittent `502` responses and slow requests. The service was deployed earlier today. You have shell access, but you should not reboot the host or blindly restart services.

## Deliverables

Produce an incident note containing:

- symptom and impact;
- timeline;
- commands run;
- evidence collected;
- hypotheses considered;
- change made;
- verification;
- prevention or follow-up.

## Phase 1: Confirm context

```bash
date
hostname
whoami
uptime
```

Confirm you are on the intended host and record the current time. Incident timelines are much easier when timestamps are explicit.

## Phase 2: Establish baseline

```bash
free -h
df -h
df -i
ss -s
systemctl --failed
```

Record anything abnormal: memory pressure, full filesystems, inode exhaustion, failed units, or unusual socket counts.

## Phase 3: Inspect the service

```bash
systemctl status api.service
systemctl cat api.service
journalctl -u api.service --since "60 minutes ago" -o short-iso
```

Determine whether the service is running, restarting, blocked on configuration, failing dependencies, or logging application errors.

## Phase 4: Follow the request path

Check from inside out:

```bash
curl -v http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
ss -lntup
ip route
cat /etc/resolv.conf
```

If there is a local proxy, inspect it too:

```bash
systemctl status nginx.service
journalctl -u nginx.service --since "60 minutes ago"
```

Separate application failure from proxy, DNS, routing, firewall, and dependency issues.

## Phase 5: Check resources and kernel signals

```bash
top
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head
dmesg -T | tail -n 100
lsof +L1
```

Look for OOM kills, high CPU loops, blocked I/O, deleted files consuming disk, and service crashes.

## Phase 6: Form hypotheses

Write at least two hypotheses before changing anything. Example:

```text
Hypothesis A: api.service cannot write because /var is full.
Evidence for: df shows /var at 100%, app logs contain ENOSPC.
Evidence against: none yet.

Hypothesis B: proxy returns 502 because app is not listening on 8080.
Evidence for: nginx logs contain connect() failed.
Evidence against: curl localhost:8080 succeeds intermittently.
```

This prevents the first plausible idea from becoming the only idea.

## Phase 7: Make one controlled change

Choose the smallest reversible change tied to evidence. Examples:

- restore a missing environment file;
- fix ownership on an application directory;
- reload a corrected proxy config;
- remove expired cache files after confirming ownership;
- restart only the failing service after preserving logs.

Avoid unrelated upgrades, cleanup, and tuning during the incident.

## Phase 8: Verify locally and externally

```bash
systemctl is-active api.service
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
journalctl -u api.service --since "5 minutes ago" -p warning..alert
```

Then verify through the user-facing path, such as the proxy or load balancer endpoint. A localhost check alone is not enough if users connect through other layers.

## Phase 9: Close the loop

Your final note should answer:

```text
What failed?
Why did it fail?
How did we know?
What changed?
How did we verify recovery?
What prevents recurrence?
```

## Graduation checklist

You should now be able to:

- navigate Linux files and permissions safely;
- reason about users, groups, and service identities;
- use streams, pipes, expansion, and text tools deliberately;
- inspect processes, sockets, logs, resources, and filesystems;
- operate systemd services with controlled changes;
- build and troubleshoot CLIs and automation;
- connect container and cloud-native symptoms back to Linux primitives;
- document production work clearly.

Mastery is not memorizing every command. It is being able to discover the right command, predict its effect, run it safely, and verify the result.
